turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hello, Dr. Smith. Well, I'm... I'm here because I am just at my wit's end, to be completely honest with you. For months now—actually, it feels like it's been building up for longer than that, but definitely for a solid few months—I’ve been trying to get people to just sit down and understand what is actually happening to me. It's my husband’s family. They are... they are quietly messing with our money and our good name, and they're doing it in this very sneaky, underhanded way so that nobody else notices. 

Like, I work as a billing clerk, right? I've been doing this a long time, I know my numbers inside and out. But lately, these little billing errors just keep showing up at work on my accounts. Just tiny things, but enough to make me look incompetent to my boss. And it’s not just at the office. It bleeds into my personal life, too. I'll go to church, and suddenly someone who has known me for a decade will just act funny toward me, give me this sideways look, or avoid me entirely, like they’ve been fed some sort of horrible lie about me. 

And the most frustrating part, the part that makes me feel like I'm just talking to a brick wall, is that no matter what records anyone pulls up—they'll say, oh, it's just a system glitch at work, or oh, so-and-so was just tired at Sunday service—I know it ties back to them. I know it does. I've been keeping track of all these little incidents, because when you put them all together, it's not just a coincidence. I know it all leads right back to his family trying to sabotage me, and I just need someone to finally listen to me and see what they are doing to my life.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a fixed, unyielding belief that her husband's family is sabotaging her work and reputation, maintaining this belief even when presented with contradictory evidence (e.g., records showing system glitches).

turns.doctor_question: Do you ever hear sounds or voices that other people around you don't seem to hear?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, definitely not. I know exactly why you're asking that, Dr. Smith, I really do. You hear what I'm saying about the sabotage and the... the coordination of it all, and people immediately just jump to, 'Oh, she must be hearing things, she must be losing her grip.' But my mind is perfectly clear, I promise you. I don't hear disembodied voices or phantom noises or anything out of the ordinary like that. 

My hearing is actually very good—almost too good sometimes, especially at the office. You know, when you work in a billing department, it's a lot of sitting in open spaces or little cubicles, and you have to learn to tune out the background hum of the copiers and the typing. But you also pick up on actual, real conversations. So if I hear someone whispering, it's a real person, flesh and blood, probably gossiping about one of those 'errors' I mentioned earlier. Or if I hear a noise, it's just someone dropping a file folder. 

But as for voices in my head or sounds that aren't actually there in the room? Absolutely not. I am dealing with real people doing real things to my life, not... not ghosts or whatever it is that makes people hear voices. I just want to be very, very clear about that, because I feel like the minute I try to explain that his family is out to get me, everyone just wants to treat me like I'm crazy. And I'm not. I'm just very observant of the actual, physical things happening around me, and I don't need to imagine voices when the real ones are already causing enough damage.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses a firm belief that her partner's family is out to get her and coordinating sabotage against her, indicating persecutory delusions.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies hearing disembodied voices, phantom noises, or sounds that aren't actually there.

turns.doctor_question: Aside from hearing things, have you ever seen anything that other people around you claim they cannot see?
turns.patient_response:
No, no, I don't see things either. It's the same thing as the hearing, Dr. Smith. I don't have hallucinations. I know that's what you're getting at—checking off the boxes for schizophrenia or something, right? I've read about how doctors evaluate these things. But I am telling you, my eyes work just fine. I wear reading glasses for the fine print on the billing statements, but otherwise, my vision is 20/20. 

I only see what is actually right in front of me. Like, if I see my sister-in-law's car parked two blocks down from my office when she has absolutely no reason to be in that part of town—which happened last Tuesday, by the way, a silver Honda Accord, I'd recognize the dent on the bumper anywhere—that's a real car. I didn't conjure it out of thin air. Or if I see my boss giving me a very specific, pitying kind of look after one of those mysterious billing errors pops up on my screen, I'm reading a real facial expression. I'm not imagining shadows in the corner of the room or people who aren't there. 

It actually really frustrates me when people try to make it about my sanity, or my eyes playing tricks on me. Because if you were in my shoes, and you saw the paperwork getting shuffled around on your desk when you *know* you left it perfectly stacked before you went to the break room to get a cup of coffee... you wouldn't think you were hallucinating, you would think someone came into your cubicle and messed with your things. Which is exactly what is happening. So no, I don't see things that aren't there. I just happen to be very, very attentive to the things that *are* there, because I have to be. If I don't pay attention to every little detail, they'll just keep getting away with it, and I can't let that happen. I just can't.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient expresses fixed, persecutory beliefs that others are intentionally messing with her paperwork, causing billing errors, and spying on her.
symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly denies experiencing visual or auditory hallucinations, stating she only sees what is actually there and does not imagine things.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you felt that your husband's family has been actively working to sabotage you in this way?
turns.patient_response:
Well, if I really sit down and trace it all back... it’s been about nine months. Yes, nine months exactly, because it all started right around the holidays last year. You know how the holidays are, they’re always a little stressful, but this was different. There was this whole... this whole big blowout with his family over money and expectations. 

They’ve always had these very rigid ideas about who should pay for what, and how we should be spending our time, and we finally had to set a boundary. We just said, 'No, we can't do it this way anymore.' And they did not like that. They smiled to our faces, of course, because that’s what they do—they’re very polite on the surface, very concerned with appearances. But that’s exactly when things started shifting. 

First, it was just little comments, you know, passive-aggressive remarks about our finances or my job. And then, a few weeks after that, right at the beginning of the year, that’s when the first billing error happened at work. I remember it so clearly because I had just finished the end-of-year reconciliation, and my numbers were perfect. Perfect. And then suddenly, this account I’ve managed for three years has a glaring discrepancy. And then another one the next week. 

So it’s been a solid nine months of this relentless... campaign. Nine months of them trying to make me look like I’m losing my mind or losing my touch at work, just because we didn't bend to their will over some holiday expenses. And it’s exhausting, Dr. Smith. Nine months of having to double-check every single keystroke, looking over my shoulder, wondering who they’ve talked to at my church, or who they’ve paid off or convinced to mess with my files. It’s a full-time job just trying to stay one step ahead of them, and it’s been going on since last winter.

symptom_reasoning.S019: The patient describes a fixed, persecutory belief that her husband's family is running a 'relentless campaign' to sabotage her work files and reputation, which has persisted for nine months.
